extracted.intended_audience: academic mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, early- to late-career faculty), especially those thinking about career balance and life management
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for mathematicians on balancing research, service, administration, teaching, outreach, and personal life across a career; includes daily time-management rules and options for mid/late-career role changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Striking a balance between research and other contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that as you age you may become less part of the mainstream research front and consider developing new interests and contributions (administration, teacher training, textbook work, outreach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter advises being of stout heart about becoming less central to cutting-edge research and instead making new contributions (e.g., running workshops for high-school teachers, consulting on textbooks, engaging in public education debates like the Math Wars). These are presented as legitimate and valuable alternatives to sustained high-intensity research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider administrative service in mid/late career
rubrics_metrics.description: As you move into your 50s, consider serving a term as Department Chair or a role such as Vice-Chair for Graduate Studies; rotating Deanships can provide limited-term administration experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serving as Chair or Dean (often term-limited/rotating) gives faculty administrative experience and can be appropriate as research intensity changes. The text specifically recommends seriously considering these options in your 50s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in education outreach and teacher support
rubrics_metrics.description: Devote time to developing fruitful relationships with local schools, teacher training, and textbook evaluation/consulting as meaningful professional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include running summer workshops for high-school teachers or serving as a go-to person for textbook comparison and consulting. Such activities are framed as important public issues that affect society and as satisfying alternatives for senior mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set realistic daily goals and stop when achieved
rubrics_metrics.description: At the beginning of each day set realistic goals; at the end of the day you should have achieved them and be able to stop working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good time management means you can leave work feeling you've done an honest day's work and can relax (dinner, concerts, reading unrelated math, planning leisure). This is an explicit rule for knowing when you are done for the day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit intense mathematical research to a few focused hours per day
rubrics_metrics.description: A recommended model is ~4–5 hours per day of intense mathematical research plus additional lighter hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests that 4–5 hours of intense work and another ~5 hours of less intense activity is more than reasonable, and that spending every waking hour on mathematics is unnecessary and unproductive. John E. Littlewood's habit of taking Sunday off is cited as an example of effective pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take regular rest (weekly rest days and breaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure you take days off (e.g., Sundays) and rest so ideas can incubate and productivity improves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Littlewood, who took Sundays off and still produced a very large body of work. Rest is framed not as laziness but as productivity-enhancing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate your professional and private personas; prioritize personal relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Strike a balance between professional obligations and family/partner/children; do not let mathematics consistently trump personal relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that habitually returning to the office after dinner sends a negative signal to partners and can harm relationships (example of a divorce where mathematics was prioritized). Advice: decide what is important and act on that insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive 'office after dinner' hours; long hours don't guarantee productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Question the habit of sitting in the office all day and returning after dinner; there is no evidence this increases productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work at home in the evenings if more convenient; prioritize effectiveness over visible hours. The author expresses skepticism that extremely long office hours translate into greater research output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use time well to maintain steady productivity and avoid neurotic overwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Good time use leads to feeling accomplished each day, prevents all-night anguishing sessions, and allows you to begin the next day fresh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is steady, sustainable productivity rather than tormented overwork. Being a mathematician should not require martyr-like suffering; moderate, focused work is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to career transitions as research intensity wanes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize alternatives to active theorem-proving such as administration, education, outreach, textbook work, and other roles that leverage mathematical expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that many senior mathematicians keep some research involvement while spending most time on other impactful activities; these are portrayed as valuable options rather than failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental and university service counts in tenure and promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Service—committee work, teaching evaluation, curriculum development, hiring and promotion activities—figures into all tenure and promotion decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The glossary explicitly notes that departmental/university service is a component considered in tenure/promotion, so faculty should account for service in career planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward system balances teaching, research, and service
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure and promotion decisions are made according to a reward system that considers teaching, research, and departmental service, with appropriate weighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty should be aware of and act according to their institution's reward system (weights may vary) and balance their efforts across these categories accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing and research productivity are central to academic advancement ('publish or perish')
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in research and publishing is typically necessary to obtain tenure and to flourish as a professor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents 'publish or perish' as a byword of American higher education, underscoring the career importance of producing and publishing original research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sabbatical opportunities (typical seven-year cycle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many institutions offer paid leave (sabbatical) roughly every seven years; at some schools it is guaranteed, at others competitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sabbaticals allow focused research or visiting other institutions and are an important career resource to plan for and use when available.
